```markdown
# groupthink

Three LLM agents answer a question, read each other's solutions, and revise. Do they end up right more often than they would by voting without talking? Where does the discussion talk a right agent out of its answer? And how far does an agent bend when two others confidently state a wrong one?

A measured study on local models (Ollama): 160 GSM8K and 160 MMLU items, two teams of three agents, two rounds of debate against a compute-matched self-revision control, and planted peers. The predictions and the analysis plan were committed before the full run ([HYPOTHESES.md](HYPOTHESES.md)), and so were the pass rules used to score them ([src/gthink/score.py](src/gthink/score.py)).

## Findings

The full run is in progress; findings land here when it ends.

## Design

- **Items:** 160 GSM8K and 160 MMLU (high-school biology, geography, macroeconomics and psychology), the seeded draws of [prompt-brittleness](https://github.com/Srikarmk/prompt-brittleness) and [format-tax](https://github.com/Srikarmk/format-tax) extended along the same permutations. Eight pilot items, used to check prompts and the parser, are excluded from every reported number.
- **Mixed team:** `qwen3:8b` (thinking off), `llama3.1:8b` and `gemma3:12b`, temperature 0, seed 7, so their disagreements are the models' own.
- **Same-model team:** `qwen3:8b` sampled three times at temperature 0.7 with seeds 1, 2 and 3, the usual setup in debate papers (Du et al., 2023).

answer: fix: correct one item misparsed in the first published version
text:
```markdown
fix: correct one item misparsed in the first published version

Found after publication, when quant-cliff re-ran the same GSM8K items: on gsm8k-0265 (gold 9,500), Llama writes "Answer: $9 500", with a space as the thousands separator, and the parser read 9. That scored a right reply wrong in Llama's round 0, A/A, planted-right and both self-revision rounds. It also changed the experiment itself: that "9" was the only wrong round-0 answer on the item, so it became the planted wrong answer, recorded as a real model mistake when it was a parsing error.

The fix: the parser joins digit groups split by a space on the answer line and inside `\boxed{}` only. No other reply in the run changes. With Llama's round 0 now right, every round-0 reply on the item is right, so its planted wrong answer is a constructed one (4,750), and the item's three planted-wrong calls were run again (the only new calls). Gemma and qwen3 kept 9,500; Llama ran to the cap without committing. The answers, report and scorecard were regenerated; the addendum above is left as it was published.
```

answer: Predictive Variance Decides: Quantitative Criterion for Region-Aware Gaussian Processes
text:
```plaintext
Predictive Variance Decides: Quantitative Criterion for Region-Aware Gaussian Processes

Allocating approximation budget unevenly across the input space --- routing ``important'' regions to high-fidelity approximations and the rest to cheap ones --- is an appealing way to scale Gaussian processes. We give a quantitative criterion for when it can work, and show the criterion is rarely satisfied.

The criterion follows from the predictive variance decomposition: sparse approximations alter only the latent term, while the shared noise term is untouched. The achievable gain from \emph{any} region-aware router is therefore bounded by the spread in predictive standard deviation across its candidate models, which is directly measurable before a router is built. On data whose regional structure is true by construction, that spread is at most $0.0017$ against a calibration error of order $0.5$ --- a ratio of $300{:}1$ --- and the criterion correctly predicts both outcomes: where the spread is negligible an oracle router given the \emph{true} generative partition gains nothing ($+0.0003$ ECE), and on the one dataset where the spread is larger ($0.064$) an oracle does gain, by the small margin the spread permits. The criterion holds from $n=600$ to $n=4800$, and the spread \emph{falls} with $n$.

We contribute three further results. (i) A measurement hazard: an opt-in fast predictive-variance setting in a widely used GP library is inert below a training-set size threshold that never appears in user code and above it perturbs predictive standard deviations by a median of ${\sim}100\%$, inflating measured ECE by $3$--$9\times$; reported calibration for ``exact'' GPs above this threshold may not describe the model. (ii) Region identification by local residual variance
